stories.headline: Update: Bodies of two missing Colorado Mountain College students found near West Apostle Mountain
stories.summary:
The bodies of two Colorado Mountain College students were found Wednesday afternoon, five days after they left Leadville for a weekend hiking trip near Huron Peak in Chaffee County, the Chaffee County Sheriff's Department said. Kaden Matsuda, 19, of Ridgway, and Jackson Donlon, 20, of New York, were found near each other in a basin of West Apostle Mountain around 3:30 p.m.

The men left Friday and told family they planned to hike Ice Mountain. A storm Saturday dropped 1 to 2 feet of snow. Family members called law enforcement Monday morning when the pair failed to return. Searchers found their vehicle at a trailhead near Winfield and later located their tent and belongings buried in snow.

Sheriff Andy Rohrich said foul play is not suspected, and that officials will not offer theories until an autopsy is completed. Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter and Donlon a mountain guide. Colorado Mountain College said it is providing emotional support to students, faculty and staff in Leadville.

stories.headline: Colorado State Capitol evacuated; suspect arrested after hoax explosive device found
stories.summary:
The Colorado State Capitol was evacuated Wednesday after Colorado State Patrol troopers found a suspicious device on a windowsill outside the building. The Denver Police Bomb Squad examined the device, which was designed to look like a bomb and was later determined not to be a threat.

The State Patrol identified a person of interest who may have had information about the device. Later in the day, the agency arrested Cody Miles Flynn, 32, on suspicion of possession of a hoax explosive device. Custody was transferred to the Denver Police Department.

The evacuation disrupted activity at the seat of state government on a day that also included events with Gov. Jared Polis. Further details on a possible motive were not immediately released.

stories.headline: Woman convicted of first-degree murder in 2025 northeast Denver shooting
stories.summary:
Ashley Stone was convicted of first-degree murder and other charges in the April 2025 shooting death of Calvin Fenner, 43, in northeast Denver, according to the Denver District Attorney's Office. She faces life in prison without the possibility of parole. Her sentencing hearing is scheduled for Nov. 25.

According to an arrest affidavit obtained by The Denver Gazette, police received a call that Stone had thrown a water bottle at a woman's vehicle and pulled a gun during school pickup. Authorities said Stone and co-defendant David Bland later pulled alongside the vehicle and fired into it, striking Fenner, who was driving. He lost consciousness and the vehicle crashed at East 38th Avenue and North Odessa Street.

The woman told police she had a brief relationship with Bland in 2023 and that Stone believed it was continuing. Bland is also charged with first-degree murder, and his trial date has not been set.

stories.headline: CDOT seeks $65 million in federal relief to repair roads after southwestern Colorado floods
stories.summary:
The Colorado Department of Transportation on Wednesday asked the Federal Highway Administration for about $65 million in Emergency Relief funds to repair highways damaged by floods in southwest Colorado. The Transportation Commission has already approved $5 million for immediate repairs.

Storms from Oct. 22 through Oct. 25 brought up to seven inches of rain in areas such as Pagosa Springs, and flooding topped four feet on some roadways. At least three highways sustained significant structural damage: US 160 over Wolf Creek Pass, US 550 on Red Mountain Pass, and CO 151, which washed out in two places. CDOT plans a temporary access road on CO 151 before permanent reconstruction.

The $65 million figure is preliminary because high water has prevented full inspections of bridges and other structures. CDOT expects a more accurate estimate in eight to 10 weeks. Gov. Jared Polis said the state wants repairs made before winter so residents can reach home, work and school.

stories.headline: Arapahoe Basin opens first, Keystone to follow, as Colorado ski season begins
stories.summary:
Arapahoe Basin in Summit County opened Wednesday, becoming the first Colorado ski area to spin lifts for the 2026-27 season. Chairlifts started about 30 minutes ahead of the announced 11 a.m. time, giving skiers access to the intermediate High Noon run via the Black Mountain Express.

Keystone Resort will open Friday from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. with more than two miles of groomed terrain on the Schoolmarm and Silver Spoon trails, plus access via the River Run Gondola. Both resorts began snowmaking Oct. 15 and ramped up as temperatures dropped this week. Last year Keystone opened Oct. 25 and A-Basin Oct. 26, so this season starts somewhat later.

A-Basin is celebrating its 80th anniversary and plans to open daily until 4 p.m. while snowmaking continues to expand terrain on the Front Side. Beaver Creek and Crested Butte have also begun snowmaking operations.

stories.headline: Democratic super PAC to spend additional $2.1 million in Colorado's 3rd District
stories.summary:
House Majority PAC, a super PAC tied to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, said Wednesday it will spend an additional $2.1 million on TV ads in Colorado's 3rd Congressional District. The money is aimed at unseating Republican Rep. Jeff Hurd, with Democrat Dwayne Romero, a former Aspen City Council member, as the challenger.

The spending comes on top of about $300,000 the group had already committed. Until this week, there had been essentially no super PAC spending on Romero's behalf. Republican groups have spent more than $3 million to benefit Hurd, including $2.5 million from two Trump-aligned super PACs that have mainly attacked Romero.

Recent polling shows the race essentially tied despite the district's Republican lean. Hurd won in 2024 by 5 points, while Donald Trump carried the district by 10. More than 1 million Colorado voters have already cast ballots.

stories.headline: RTD moves ahead with scaled-back L-Line upgrades in Five Points
stories.summary:
The Regional Transportation District is proceeding with a modified plan to repair and upgrade parts of the L-Line rather than fully reconstruct it, as Denver officials work on options for the Welton Street corridor in Five Points. RTD staff presented the plan at Tuesday's Board of Directors meeting, for discussion only, since funding for the Downtown Rail Reconstruction Project was already approved.

The plan would cover Americans with Disabilities Act and safety upgrades at stations and replace sections of rail and pavement. Staff said it should keep the line operating for another 15 years. Some directors, including JoyAnn Ruscha, voiced concern about waiting on the city to decide the corridor's layout.

Five Points residents say the current configuration squeezes pedestrians against the train, limits service because one track serves both directions, and restricts sidewalk space. Denver expects to finalize a preferred transit alternative for Welton Street by next summer.

stories.headline: Northbound I-25 to close overnight in Lone Tree for pedestrian bridge work
stories.summary:
The Colorado Department of Transportation will close northbound Interstate 25 in Lone Tree on Wednesday and Thursday nights so crews can finish installing a pedestrian bridge. Traffic impacts begin Wednesday at 3 p.m. with closure of the off-ramp to Lincoln Avenue.

All northbound lanes between Ridgegate Parkway and Lincoln Avenue will close at 10 p.m. each night and reopen at 5 a.m. the following morning. Lane closures begin at 6 p.m. Wednesday and 8 p.m. Thursday. Drivers will be detoured onto Ridgegate Parkway, east to South Peoria Street, north to Lincoln Avenue and back onto I-25.

Crews had to close the highway again after complications installing the southbound bridge section Monday and Tuesday. The northbound section is scheduled for installation this week, weather permitting. Updated information is available at cotrip.org.

stories.headline: Committee recommends revoking approval for $300M Broomfield Town Square project
stories.summary:
A Broomfield city committee has recommended that the city and county government revoke the site development plan for the $300 million Broomfield Town Square project. The recommendation follows a permit dispute with the project's developers.

The developers have sued Broomfield over permit requirements for the project. The committee's recommendation adds a new development to the dispute, though the full governing body must still act on it.

stories.headline: Colorado executives expect growth but sour on business climate, survey finds
stories.summary:
A new survey of top Colorado executives finds that many expect the state's business climate to worsen even as 57% anticipate sales growth. The survey examines the disconnect between those two outlooks.

The findings also address executives' views on the potential impacts of Amendment 87, an income tax measure on the November ballot.

stories.headline: Wayfair plans outlet store at Aurora's Southlands shopping center
stories.summary:
Wayfair plans to open its first Mountain West store at Denver's Avenues at Northfield this fall. An outlet store at Aurora's Southlands Shopping Center is expected shortly after.

Separately, PepsiCo's 1.25 million-square-foot bottling plant near Denver International Airport is operating under temporary certificates while the company explores further expansion. Two companies also purchased a retail center that houses a 1,100-seat restaurant with cliff divers, and upgrades are planned.

stories.headline: Broncos' Alex Singleton named AFC Defensive Player of the Week
stories.summary:
Denver Broncos inside linebacker Alex Singleton was named AFC Defensive Player of the Week by the NFL on Wednesday for his performance in the team's Week 7 win over Arizona. It is the first such honor of his eight-year career.

The Broncos improved to 5-2 and sit second in the AFC West. Analysts have pointed to quarterback Bo Nix and the passing game as key to the win.

Denver now turns to a Week 8 matchup with the Kansas City Chiefs at Empower Field at Mile High on Sunday.

topStory.headline: At Least 69 Killed When Two High-Speed Trains Collide South of Madrid
topStory.summary:
Two high-speed trains collided Wednesday morning on the Madrid-to-Seville line near the town of Urda, in Spain's Castilla-La Mancha region, killing at least 69 people according to the BBC. The Guardian reported at least 68 dead and dozens more injured. The crash occurred at 8:53 a.m. local time between the municipalities of Mora and Orgaz, about 140 kilometers south of Madrid, when a state-operated Renfe train struck the back of a stationary train run by the private company Iryo. Some carriages fell down an embankment, and all traffic on the line was halted, with Renfe suspending services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Transport Minister Óscar Puente said a computer failure at about 8:30 a.m. initially halted six moving trains, including the two that later collided. He said the rail control center, which takes over in the event of a system failure, decided to let the trains move again without speed restrictions, a decision he described as made "under inexplicable circumstances." Iryo said its train was struck from behind by a Renfe train "due to causes that are still unknown."

Audio recordings obtained by Spanish media appear to show a controller at the infrastructure company Adif clearing one train to move at 8:36 a.m., even though another train about 25 kilometers ahead had stalled. In one recording, the controller tells the Renfe driver to disconnect and reconnect the LZB speed-monitoring system and proceed under the Lateral Signalling Block, a backup system, "at normal speed." The driver asks, "At normal speed?" and the controller answers, "Yes." Under normal protocols, a driver in that situation would be expected to travel at no more than 40 km/h by line of sight, rather than at normal speed on a track designed for up to 200 km/h. In a second recording, the Iryo driver reports the train is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda.

Survivors described scenes of severe injury. Josimar Medina, a 37-year-old Peruvian tourist in the seventh carriage of the Renfe train, said he was thrown through the air and saw people with severe injuries, and he helped an injured young American man to safety. Fredrich and Arabella Barilea, a couple from the Philippines living in Dubai who were on the Iryo train, said passengers shouted warnings that another train could hit and fled the wreckage. Urda became an emergency response hub, with a local sports center used as a triage post and emergency vehicles arriving from Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid.

Officials have begun visiting the area. Interior Minister Fernando Grande Marlaska and Castilla-La Mancha regional president Emiliano García-Page visited the emergency coordination center near the site, and opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo arrived later. The cause remains under investigation, with attention focused on the control center's decision to restore normal-speed movement after the system failure and on the signalling systems involved. The death toll could change as rescue and recovery work continues.
